claim: The little skate Leucoraja erinacea shares a common ancestor with tetrapods 473 MYA.
source: The little skate Leucoraja erinacea is a marine species of jawed vertebrate which shares a common ancestor with tetrapods 473 MYA (Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: The little skate displays a walking-like behavior which resembles limb-based locomotion.
source: Yet, it displays a walking-like behavior which resembles limb-based locomotion (Holst and Bone, 1993; Koester et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holst and Bone, 1993; Koester et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2018.

claim: The genetic programs and neural subtypes essential for walking existed in a common ancestor of cartilaginous fish and tetrapods.
source: Yet, it displays a walking-like behavior which resembles limb-based locomotion (Holst and Bone, 1993; Koester et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2018), suggesting that the genetic programs and neural subtypes essential for walking existed in a common ancestor of cartilaginous fish and tetrapods.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of walking-like behavior in little skate and supported by citations.

claim: Little skate pectoral and pelvic fin MNs express forelimb MN Hox genes, Hoxa6/7 and a hindlimb MN Hox gene, Hoxa10, respectively.
source: Little skate pectoral and pelvic fin MNs express forelimb MN Hox genes, Hoxa6/7 and a hindlimb MN Hox gene, Hoxa10, respectively.
evidence: The claim is stated as a finding from previous developmental studies on the little skate.

claim: The little skate genome lacks the Hoxc cluster.
source: In addition, the little skate genome lacks the Hoxc cluster (King et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to King et al., 2011.

claim: The little skate spinal cord is occupied by fin MNs without an inter-fin region.
source: and its spinal cord is occupied by fin MNs without an inter-fin region, which is reminiscent of the Hoxc cluster mutant mouse (Jung et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 2014.

claim: Little skate has ~10 pelvic fin muscles.
source: However, the mechanisms that regulate expression of genes controlling motor circuit development remain to be identified, and how different species generate MN subtypes to innervate ~10 pelvic fin muscles of little skate (Macesic and Kajiura, 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Macesic and Kajiura, 2010.

claim: Tetrapods have ~50 limb muscles.
source: versus ~50 limb muscles of tetrapods (Sweeney et al., 2018; Landmesser, 1978; Sullivan, 1962)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sweeney et al., 2018; Landmesser, 1978; Sullivan, 1962.

claim: The previous little skate reference genome was severely fragmented.
source: However, in little skate, such genome-wide omics studies have been limited due to severe fragmentation of the reference genome (Wyffels et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wyffels et al., 2014.

claim: A new genome assembly of 2.13 Gb was generated for little skate.
source: Here, we generated a new genome assembly of 2.13 Gb and gene annotation of little skate by applying a combination of PacBio long-read and Illumina short-read sequencing analyses
evidence: The claim is stated as a result of the study and supported by the assembly statistics shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The new little skate genome assembly increased by 36.5% compared to the previous assembly.
source: Compared to the previous assembly, our assembled genome size increased by 36.5%–2.13 Gb (Wyffels et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with the previous assembly data from Wyffels et al., 2014.

claim: The new little skate genome assembly represents ~93% of the estimated genome size based on K-mer spectra.
source: ~93% of the estimated genome size based on K-mer spectra of whole genome sequencing data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by K-mer analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The contiguity of the new little skate genome was improved by over 300-fold in terms of contig N50 of 214 Kb.
source: The contiguity of the genome was also improved by over 300-fold, in terms of contig N50 of 214 Kb.
evidence: The claim is supported by assembly statistics comparing the new and old assemblies.

claim: Missing and fragmented BUSCO genes were reduced to 7.3% and 3.6% in the new assembly, respectively.
source: Missing and fragmented BUSCO which was 69.1% and 23.9% in the previous assembly has been reduced to 7.3% and 3.6% in our assembly, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis comparing the new and old assemblies.

claim: The proportion of complete BUSCO genes in the new assembly is 89.1%.
source: Also, the proportion of complete BUSCO genes (89.1%) as well as the long transcript lengths demonstrate improved completeness than that of the previous assembly (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Approximately 63.6% of the little skate genome is occupied by repetitive elements.
source: Approximately, 63.6% of the little skate genome is occupied by repetitive elements (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE) were the most abundant of all repeat classes in the little skate genome.
source: Among the repeats, long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE) were the most abundant of all classes which is similar to thorny skate and three shark genome assemblies (Hara et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat analysis and comparison with other species, with citation to Hara et al., 2018.

claim: The scaffold N50 of the new little skate genome assembly is 61.3 Mb.
source: A scaffold N50 of 61.3 Mb of our little skate genome assembly was comparable to a recently published high-quality thorny skate genome assembly (Rhie et al., 2021; 62.1 Mb; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by assembly statistics shown in Figure 1B and comparison with thorny skate genome.

claim: The number of protein-coding genes predicted in the new little skate genome assembly is 17,230.
source: The number of protein-coding genes (17,230) and transcripts (17,952) predicted in the new genome assembly was similar to the number in the thorny skate genome (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene annotation statistics shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of transcripts predicted in the new little skate genome assembly is 17,952.
source: The number of protein-coding genes (17,230) and transcripts (17,952) predicted in the new genome assembly was similar to the number in the thorny skate genome (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene annotation statistics shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Coding sequences in the assembled Hoxa cluster aligned well with the fully sequenced BAC clone.
source: Coding sequences in our assembled Hoxa cluster aligned well with the fully sequenced BAC clone (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), highlighting the reliability of the new assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Complete loss of Hoxc cluster was observed in the little skate genome.
source: We observed complete loss of Hoxc cluster in the little skate genome which was also shown in the thorny skate genome (King et al., 2011; Rhie et al., 2021; Criswell et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by genome analysis and citations to King et al., 2011; Rhie et al., 2021; Criswell et al., 2021.

claim: The BUSCO gene synteny of little skate showed more similar patterns with chicken and mammals than with zebrafish.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that the BUSCO gene synteny of little skate showed more similar patterns with chicken and mammals than with zebrafish (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: One CTCF site located between Hoxa7 and Hoxa9, and between Hoxa10 and Hoxa11 were conserved across diverse species and were also observed in little skate Hoxa cluster.
source: Among previously reported CTCF sites in mouse (Narendra et al., 2015), one located between Hoxa7 and Hoxa9, and between Hoxa10 and Hoxa11 were conserved across diverse species and were also observed in little skate Hoxa cluster despite the phylogenetic distance (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CTCF motif analysis shown in Figure 1D and citation to Narendra et al., 2015.

claim: The CTCF motifs near Hoxa13 upstream and between Hoxa5 and Hoxa6 which are conserved in other species were not found in putative CTCF sites of skate, elephant shark, and other sharks.
source: On the other hand, the CTCF motifs near Hoxa13 upstream and between Hoxa5 and Hoxa6 which are conserved in other species were not found in putative CTCF sites of skate, elephant shark, and other sharks reported previously (Hara et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by CTCF motif analysis and citation to Hara et al., 2018.

claim: The absence of the CTCF site between Hoxa5 and Hoxa6 may contribute to the relatively expanded domain of Hoxa9 in fin innervating MNs.
source: The absence of the CTCF site between Hoxa5 and Hoxa6 may contribute to the relatively expanded domain of Hoxa9 in fin innervating MNs (Jung et al., 2018; Narendra et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Jung et al., 2018; Narendra et al., 2015.

claim: Comparing the expression of 10,270 genes in pectoral fin MNs with tail-region spinal cord identified 411 differentially expressed genes.
source: Comparing the expression of 10,270 genes in pectoral fin MNs (pec-MNs) with tail-region spinal cord (tail-SC) identified 411 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) including 135 genes upregulated in the pec-MNs and 276 genes in the tail-SC (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: 135 genes were upregulated in the pec-MNs.
source: Comparing the expression of 10,270 genes in pectoral fin MNs (pec-MNs) with tail-region spinal cord (tail-SC) identified 411 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) including 135 genes upregulated in the pec-MNs and 276 genes in the tail-SC (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: 276 genes were upregulated in the tail-SC.
source: Comparing the expression of 10,270 genes in pectoral fin MNs (pec-MNs) with tail-region spinal cord (tail-SC) identified 411 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) including 135 genes upregulated in the pec-MNs and 276 genes in the tail-SC (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larger number of DEGs in tail-SC may be caused by comparing heterogeneous cell types in tail-SC with homogeneous cell type in pec-MNs.
source: Larger number of DEGs in tail-SC may be caused by comparing heterogeneous cell types in tail-SC with homogeneous cell type in pec-MNs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the observed data.

claim: A rostral Hox gene, Hoxa7 was highly expressed in pec-MNs.
source: while a rostral Hox gene, Hoxa7 was highly expressed in pec-MNs (Figure 2B), which is consistent with previous immunohistochemical analyses (Jung et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation to Jung et al., 2018.

claim: A greater number of mouse MN-expressed genes were highly expressed in pec-MNs (enriched in pec-MN, 17 genes; enriched in tail-SC, 9 genes; fold difference (FD) ≥2).
source: Overall, we observed a greater number of mouse MN-expressed genes were highly expressed in pec-MNs (enriched in pec-MN, 17 genes; enriched in tail-SC, 9 genes; fold difference (FD) ≥2; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A greater number of interneuron markers was observed in tail-SC (enriched in tail-SC, 29 genes; enriched in pec-MNs, 8 genes; FD ≥2).
source: On the other hand, a greater number of interneuron markers was observed in tail-SC (enriched in tail-SC, 29 genes; enriched in pec-MNs, 8 genes; FD ≥2), which is composed predominantly of interneuron cell-types.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression analysis.

claim: 1038 genes were commonly found in mouse, little skate and chick MNs.
source: Among shared genes, 1038 genes were commonly found in mouse, little skate and chick, while 63, 36, and 24 genes were identified in the little skate-mouse pair, little skate-chick pair and mouse-chick pair, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 53, 32, and 7 genes were highly expressed (percentile >70) in MNs of little skate, mouse and chick with almost no expression in the remaining species (percentile <30).
source: Species-specific genes were also identified; 53, 32, and 7 genes were highly expressed (percentile >70) in MNs of little skate, mouse and chick with almost no expression in the remaining species (percentile <30), which suggest that the genes are expressed in MNs of one species but not in MNs of other species at the similar developmental stages (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 12, 171, and 6 paralog genes were specifically expressed by skate, mouse and chicken MNs, respectively.
source: In addition to the comparisons among ortholog genes, we also identified 12, 171, and 6 paralog genes specifically expressed by skate, mouse and chicken MNs, respectively which could further explain species-specific differences of MNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B; Supplementary files 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by paralog gene analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A total of 61,997 consensus accessible chromatin regions (ACRs) were identified in fin-MNs and tail-SC.
source: Through peak calling, a total of 61,997 consensus accessible chromatin regions (ACRs) were identified in fin-MNs and tail-SC, indicated by intense red color in the heatmap (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 7869 ACRs were found in both fin-MNs and tail-SC.
source: Among them, 7869 ACRs were found in both fin-MNs and tail-SC while 35,741 and 18,387 ACRs were found only in fin-MNs and tail-SC, respectively (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 35,741 ACRs were found only in fin-MNs.
source: Among them, 7869 ACRs were found in both fin-MNs and tail-SC while 35,741 and 18,387 ACRs were found only in fin-MNs and tail-SC, respectively (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 18,387 ACRs were found only in tail-SC.
source: Among them, 7869 ACRs were found in both fin-MNs and tail-SC while 35,741 and 18,387 ACRs were found only in fin-MNs and tail-SC, respectively (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Many ACRs were found in intron and intergenic regions for all ACR types (intron, 35.0%; intergenic region, 45.1%).
source: The genome-wide distribution analysis of ACRs showed that many ACRs were found in intron and intergenic regions for all ACR types (intron, 35.0%; intergenic region, 45.1%; Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by ACR distribution analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The density of ACRs was found to be highest in promoters and 5'UTRs.
source: however, normalizing each region by its length, the density of ACRs was found to be highest in promoters and 5'UTRs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ACR density analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Genes with greater depth of ATAC-seq in their promoter region are generally expressed at higher levels than those genes with closed chromatin form in both fin-MNs and tail-SC.
source: As a result, we found that the genes with greater depth of ATAC-seq in their promoter region are generally expressed at higher levels than those genes with closed chromatin form in both fin-MNs and tail-SC (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 19, 25, and 32 TF motif predictions were found in fin-MN-specific ACRs, shared and tail-SC-specific ACRs, respectively.
source: Overall, 19, 25, and 32 TF motif predictions were found in fin-MN-specific ACRs, shared and tail-SC-specific ACRs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Fin-MN-specific ACRs were enriched with predicted motifs of Hoxa5 and Hoxd9, which are expressed in the fin-MNs of little skate.
source: Fin-MN-specific ACRs were enriched with predicted motifs of Hoxa5 and Hoxd9, which are expressed in the fin-MNs of little skate, while the tail-SC-specific ACRs were enriched with the predicted motifs of Hoxd11 and Hoxa13, expressed in tail SCs of little skate (Jung et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis and citation to Jung et al., 2018.

claim: Tail-SC-specific ACRs were enriched with the predicted motifs of Hoxd11 and Hoxa13, expressed in tail SCs of little skate.
source: Fin-MN-specific ACRs were enriched with predicted motifs of Hoxa5 and Hoxd9, which are expressed in the fin-MNs of little skate, while the tail-SC-specific ACRs were enriched with the predicted motifs of Hoxd11 and Hoxa13, expressed in tail SCs of little skate (Jung et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis and citation to Jung et al., 2018.

claim: Motif predictions of Foxp1, Pbx1, and Lhx3, well-known regulators in MN, were found in the ACRs.
source: In addition, motif predictions of Foxp1, Pbx1, and Lhx3, well-known regulators in MN (Dasen et al., 2008; Hanley et al., 2016; Thaler et al., 2002), were found in the ACRs
evidence: The claim is supported by TF motif enrichment analysis and citations to Dasen et al., 2008; Hanley et al., 2016; Thaler et al., 2002.

claim: A larger number of TF motif predictions were found in mouse (115) compared to skate (Howe et al., 2013).
source: Among the ACRs of skate pec-MN and mouse limb-level MN-expressed genes (percentile >70; Figure 5), a larger number of TF motif predictions were found in mouse (115) compared to skate (Howe et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative TF motif analysis and citation to Howe et al., 2013.

claim: 14 TF motifs were commonly found in both mouse limb-level and skate fin MN ACRs.
source: Among the motif predictions, 14 TF motifs were commonly found in both mouse limb-level and skate fin MN ACRs (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative TF motif analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Only a subset of the 14 TF motifs (10 TF motifs, PV interneurons; 8 TF motifs, excitatory neurons) were enriched in ACRs of genes expressed in cortical PV interneuron and excitatory neurons.
source: while only a subset of the 14 TF motifs (10 TF motifs, PV interneurons; 8 TF motifs, excitatory neurons) were enriched in ACRs of genes expressed in cortical PV interneuron and excitatory neurons (Mo et al., 2015; Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative TF motif analysis shown in Figure 5C and citation to Mo et al., 2015.

claim: Motif predictions of Pknox1, Pbx3, Hoxa5, and Cux1 were found in ACRs of genes expressed in skate fin MNs and mouse limb-level MNs but not in the neurons of the brain.
source: Motif predictions of Pknox1, Pbx3, Hoxa5, and Cux1 were found in ACRs of genes expressed in skate fin MNs and mouse limb-level MNs but not in the neurons of the brain, which suggests that the shared TF motifs were not randomly observed, and the shared TF motifs may have functions in regulating cell type or regional identities of neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative TF motif analysis and inference about their function.

claim: A significantly greater number of predicted TF motifs were found in mouse MNs than in skate MNs in the ACRs of the highly expressed genes in MNs (percentile >70).
source: In the ACRs of the highly expressed genes in MNs (percentile >70), we found a significantly greater number of predicted TF motifs in mouse MNs than in skate MNs (Figure 5D and E)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative TF motif analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The greater number of predicted TFs would potentially bind to and regulate the expression of genes expressed in mouse limb-level MNs compared to skate fin MNs.
source: suggesting that the greater number of predicted TFs would potentially bind to and regulate the expression of genes expressed in mouse limb-level MNs compared to skate fin MNs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: Foxp1 is expressed in and required for the specification of all limb MNs in tetrapods.
source: Although Foxp1 is expressed in and required for the specification of all limb MNs in tetrapods, Foxp1 is downregulated in Pea3-positive MN pools during maturation in mice (Dasen et al., 2008; Catela et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2008; Catela et al., 2016.

claim: Foxp1 is downregulated in Pea3-positive MN pools during maturation in mice.
source: Although Foxp1 is expressed in and required for the specification of all limb MNs in tetrapods, Foxp1 is downregulated in Pea3-positive MN pools during maturation in mice (Dasen et al., 2008; Catela et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2008; Catela et al., 2016.

claim: Preganglionic motor column neurons (PGC MNs) in the thoracic spinal cord of mouse and chick express less than half the level of Foxp1 expression in limb MNs.
source: In addition, preganglionic motor column neurons (PGC MNs) in the thoracic spinal cord of mouse and chick express less than half the level of Foxp1 expression in limb MNs.
evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Foxp1 is not expressed in MNs that express pSmad in little skate.
source: We observed that Foxp1 is not expressed in MNs that express pSmad (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The top 49 scaffolds constituted 97.8% of the little skate genome.
source: The 49 scaffolds constituted 97.8% of the little skate genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by assembly statistics.

claim: Marletaz et al. generated a new chromosome-scale genome via combination of Pacbio, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing.
source: Marletaz et al. generated a new chromosome-scale genome via combination of Pacbio, Illumina and Hi-C sequencing.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact about another study.
